passage:
At lunch break, Harsha opened his steel tiffin. Beside him, Omkar was staring at the window with nothing on his desk.
"Where's your tiffin?" Harsha whispered.
"Forgot it. It's okay."
"You're not eating anything?"
"I'll drink water."
Harsha looked at his lemon rice. Mum always packed a lot. "Here," he said, pushing the lid across. "Take half."
"Really? It's yours."
"There's too much. Just take it. Use my spoon, I have another."
Omkar hesitated, then scooped some rice onto the lid. "Thanks, Harsha. This is really good."
"Mum puts peanuts in it."
Harsha ate his half slowly. His stomach felt a little empty, but warm all the same. When Omkar laughed at a joke at the back of the class, Harsha smiled to himself.

qa.q: What food did Harsha share with Omkar?
qa.a: Harsha shared half of his lemon rice.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel after giving half of his lunch?
qa.a: He felt warm and content, even though his stomach was a little empty. He smiled to himself when Omkar laughed.

qa.q: What could Omkar do to keep the friendship fair if a lunch is ever forgotten again?
qa.a: Omkar could say thank you again, and another day bring something to share with Harsha, so giving goes both ways. 😊

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt when Omkar said it was okay and would just drink water?
qa.a: Omkar may have felt embarrassed or shy about not having food, and not wanting to be a bother. Harsha's easy offer let Omkar accept without feeling small.

grounding: A child gives half his tiffin to a hungry classmate without being told and feels warm afterwards.

passage:
At recess I noticed Amandeep sitting alone on the steps by the bus lane. Everyone else was eating. His hands were in his lap, and he was watching the ants.
I had two parathas that day. Nobody had told me to do anything. I just thought that my stomach was full and his wasn't. So I walked over and tore one paratha in half. "Want this?" I said.
He looked surprised. "You sure?" I nodded. He ate it fast, then said thanks in a small voice.
I didn't tell anyone. Afterwards I felt light, like when you run and stop. I started looking for who else was sitting alone. I'm Rafiq, and that was the first time I noticed that I liked giving.

qa.q: What did Rafiq give to Amandeep?
qa.a: Rafiq tore one of his two parathas in half and gave it to Amandeep.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel after giving away half a paratha?
qa.a: Rafiq felt light and glad, like after running and stopping, and began noticing who else was sitting alone.

qa.q: What could Rafiq do next if he wants to keep helping Amandeep without making him feel embarrassed?
qa.a: Rafiq could sit with Amandeep and share casually, as before. Asking Amandeep to play afterwards would help him feel included, not pitied.

qa.q: What was it like for Amandeep when Rafiq walked over?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and hungry, and maybe a little shy. He asked "You sure?" and ate quickly, which shows the food mattered to him.

grounding: A child gives half a lunch to a hungry classmate unprompted and feels warm afterwards, starting to see the narrator as someone who gives.

passage: It was drizzling in Lisbon, and Beatriz's lunch had fallen into a puddle on the way to school. At break she sat on the bench with nothing, arms crossed, pretending not to care. Mina noticed. Nobody told her to do anything. She opened her box, looked at her cheese sandwich, and tore it carefully down the middle. "Here. The bigger half's yours, I had a big breakfast." Beatriz blinked, then smiled and took it. They ate together under the covered walkway, crumbs everywhere. Walking back to class, Mina felt a warm, fizzy feeling in her chest. At home that evening she told her mother, "I think I'm a sharing sort of person." Her mother laughed and asked why. Mina told her the whole story, twice.

qa.q: What happened to Beatriz's lunch?
qa.a: It had fallen into a puddle on the way to school.

qa.q: What was Mina feeling as she walked back to class?
qa.a: She felt warm and happy, a fizzy feeling in her chest after sharing her sandwich.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering the bigger half with a light excuse worked, because Beatriz could accept the food without feeling embarrassed.

qa.q: How might Beatriz have felt before Mina came over?
qa.a: Beatriz was probably hungry and embarrassed, crossing her arms and pretending not to care.

grounding: Shows a child freely sharing lunch with a classmate who has none, feeling warm afterwards and starting to see herself as generous.

passage: Pallavi saw Nazia open her empty bag at lunch break in Class 5B and go pink. "Forgot my tiffin. Mummy left early for the hospital shift." Around them, the classroom filled with smells of dal and parathas. Nobody had said a word to Pallavi, but she pushed her steel box across. "Take two parathas. I've got four, I can't finish." Nazia hesitated, then took them. "Thank you." "With the pickle, it's better," Pallavi said. The rest of the day, Pallavi kept smiling at nothing. When the teacher asked the class to write one good thing they did this week, she wrote about the parathas without even thinking.

qa.q: Why did Nazia forget her tiffin?
qa.a: Her Mummy left early for the hospital shift.

qa.q: How can you tell Pallavi felt good after sharing?
qa.a: She kept smiling at nothing for the rest of the day and chose the parathas as her good deed without even thinking, which shows she felt proud and warm.

qa.q: What small step helped Nazia accept the food easily?
qa.a: Pallavi said she had four and couldn't finish, and offered the pickle too, which made taking the food feel ordinary rather than like charity.

qa.q: What was it like for Nazia when she opened her empty bag?
qa.a: She went pink, so she was probably embarrassed and worried about going hungry in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a child freely sharing half her lunch with a classmate without being asked, and feeling warm about it afterwards.

passage:
Tuesday: Binita noticed Bidisha sitting on the steps at lunch, not eating. "My mother's got the new baby, she forgot to pack," Bidisha said, shrugging. Binita ate her luchi fast and felt oddly bad about it.
Wednesday: Same steps. This time Binita sat down and split her tiffin before she could think. "Half-half." Bidisha grinned. Binita felt warm all through maths.
The next Monday: Binita asked her Ma, all by herself, to pack a little extra "just in case." Ma raised an eyebrow. "For who?" "For whoever needs it. I'm good at sharing now," Binita said, and Ma smiled.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha have no lunch on Tuesday?
qa.a: Her mother had the new baby and forgot to pack.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling on Tuesday after eating fast?
qa.a: She felt oddly bad, a small guilty pang at eating while Bidisha had nothing.

qa.q: What would you advise Binita if Bidisha keeps coming without lunch?
qa.a: Keep sharing kindly, and also mention it to Ma or the class teacher so an adult can check the family is managing with the new baby.

qa.q: How might Ma see Binita's request for extra food?
qa.a: Ma is surprised at first but seems pleased and proud that Binita thought of it on her own.

grounding: Shows a child moving from noticing a hungry classmate to freely sharing and then seeing herself as someone who gives.

passage: Kamal, you asked why I always pack an extra roti. When I was nine, at the municipal school near the mill, there was a boy called Bhola who never opened a tiffin. One day his stomach growled so loudly the whole row laughed. At lunch I didn't ask anyone. I tore my paratha in half, put it on his slate, and went back to my place. He didn't say thank you. He just ate, very fast. I walked home that day feeling taller, warm right through, though I was hungry by evening. Nobody told me to do it again, but I did, most days, till the term ended. After that, your Nilesh Dadu was "the one who shares" in his own head. Sixty years later, I still am.

qa.q: What did Nilesh put on Bhola's slate?
qa.a: He put half of his paratha on it.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel walking home that day?
qa.a: He felt warm right through and proud, "taller", even though he was hungry by evening 😊

qa.q: Why did Nilesh's choice at lunch matter so much, in the story?
qa.a: No one told him to share, so the choice was his own, and repeating it made him see himself as someone who shares.

qa.q: How might Bhola have felt when the paratha appeared on his slate?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved and a little embarrassed after the laughing, which could be why he ate fast without saying thank you.

grounding: Shows a child freely giving half his lunch to a hungry classmate and growing a lasting sense of himself as generous.
